Clara Raises $105 Million: The Race to Reinvent Corporate Finance in Latin America

The future of fintech may not be built around consumer payments alone. Increasingly, investors are backing platforms that help businesses manage the complexity of money itself.

Clara, a five-year-old São Paulo-based fintech startup, has secured $105 million in fresh financing to expand its corporate financial management business.

The funding comprises a $65 million Series C round anchored by Citius, Kaszek Ventures, and DEG, alongside $40 million in renewed growth financing from General Catalyst's Customer Value Fund.

Clara helps businesses manage corporate spending, invoices, bills, and cross-border payments through an integrated financial platform.

The problem it is addressing is significant. Businesses operating across Latin America often navigate fragmented payment systems, complex financial administration, and cross-border transaction challenges.

Clara's proposition is to bring these financial operations together, giving companies greater visibility and control over their spending.

But the bigger story is the growing confidence of investors in Latin America's fintech infrastructure.

While much of the global AI and technology conversation focuses on consumer-facing applications, companies like Clara are targeting the operational foundations of business: payments, financial visibility, expense management, and cash-flow efficiency.

For emerging markets, this development carries an important lesson.

The next generation of valuable fintech companies may not simply be those helping people move money. They may be the companies rebuilding how businesses manage, monitor, and deploy capital.

The future of fintech belongs to platforms that solve real financial infrastructure problems, not just those that make transactions faster.

content:
Is fintech funding making a comeback?

After a challenging few years for investment markets, the latest numbers suggest confidence is returning to the sector.

Global fintech funding grew 35% year-on-year in Q3, driven by a surge in funding rounds exceeding $100m. 

What stands out isn't just the increase in capital.

It's where that capital is flowing.

Large investors appear to be backing fewer, bigger opportunities, signalling renewed confidence in fintech businesses that have proven scale, strong economics and a clear path to growth. 

For founders, this creates both an opportunity and a challenge:
✅ More capital is available for the right businesses
✅ Investor confidence is recovering
❌ Competition for larger rounds remains intense
❌ Expectations around profitability and execution are higher than ever

The bigger question for the industry is whether this marks the start of a sustained recovery or simply reflects investor appetite for a small number of standout fintechs.

As we head into 2027, it'll be fascinating to see whether funding strength broadens across the ecosystem or remains concentrated in the largest deals.

Are we witnessing the return of fintech's growth cycle, or is investment becoming increasingly focused on a handful of market leaders?

content:
The most important number in modern macroeconomics is unexplained.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics went to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford for the microfoundations of macroeconomic stabilisation. Embedded in that work is a finding every central bank now models: roughly 80% of households behave as forward-looking consumers. The other 20% live hand-to-mouth.

Nobel-anchored. Estimable. Stable across countries. But taken as a brute fact — never explained.

Our new working paper asks the prior question: what makes a household hand-to-mouth?
Not income. Two households at identical income differ in what they can feasibly do — health, housing burden, credit access, mobility — before any decision is made. Our claim: the 80/20 split is a measurable signature of underlying capability heterogeneity. And because it varies across countries and time, its covariates can be estimated. Capability becomes a variable, not a metaphor.

Why it matters:

▪ The same shock doesn't act on a representative agent — it acts on a distribution of capacities to adjust.
▪ Your workforce sits in that distribution — participation, absenteeism, benefit exposure.
▪ Capability gets priced as a reduction in future liabilities — the bridge between capability and capital.

The mechanism is set out in our SSRN paper The Household Affordability Frontier: structural costs form a threshold beyond which households optimise for survival rather than invest in capability — the frontier we argue produces the split itself.

An extension claim, not a rival claim. We accept the microfoundations revolution in full — and ask what produces the deciders.

content:
التحليل الجزئي والكلي 📊
Micro-economic Analysis & Macro-economic Analysis

يُعرف التحليل الاقتصادي بأنه أسلوب علمي يتعرف به على العوامل المؤثرة في الظواهر والمسائل الاقتصادية، ويفسّر أسبابها، ويستخلص منه النظريات والقوانين الاقتصادية.

وينقسم إلى قسمين متكاملين:
🔹 التحليل الجزئي (Micro-economic Analysis): يدرس الوحدات الاقتصادية الفردية، كالمستهلك والمنشأة والسوق، وقضايا تشكيل أسعار السلع والخدمات.
🔹 التحليل الكلي (Macro-economic Analysis): يدرس الاقتصاد الوطني ككل، ومنه الدخل القومي والبطالة والتضخم والاستثمار.

وهذا يقودنا إلى مغالطة مهمة: ما يصح على الفرد لا يصح بالضرورة على المجتمع. فالادخار الفردي مفيد، لكن إذا ادّخر الجميع وتوقف الإنفاق، انخفض الطلب الكلي، ثم الإنتاج والدخل القومي.

📘 المصطلحات:
Micro-economic Analysis = التحليل الجزئي
Macro-economic Analysis = التحليل الكلي
Fallacy of Composition = مغالطة التركيب

🔊 النطق: «ميكرو إيكونوميك أناليسيس» · «ماكرو إيكونوميك أناليسيس» · «فالاسي أوف كومبوزيشن»

Micro-economic and Macro-economic Analysis 📊

Economic analysis is a scientific method for identifying the factors that influence economic phenomena and problems, explaining their causes, and deriving theories and laws from them.

It divides into two complementary parts:
🔹 Micro-economic Analysis: studies individual economic units such as the consumer, the firm and the market, and how prices of goods and services are formed.
🔹 Macro-economic Analysis: studies the national economy as a whole, including national income, unemployment, inflation and investment.

This leads to an important fallacy: what holds for the individual does not necessarily hold for society. Individual saving is useful, but if everyone saves and spending stops, total demand falls, then production and national income.

📘 Key terms:
Micro-economic Analysis = التحليل الجزئي
Macro-economic Analysis = التحليل الكلي
Fallacy of Composition = مغالطة التركيب

The #AI revolution in economics itself is still in its Kaffeehaus stage. Everyone knows something is brewing. It is talked about a lot. Some experiment with revolution in a safe space. Some are a bit afraid of taking on the old order, everyone knows it cannot last. 

I came away a bit more optimistic for humans. AI can do a lot, but it is the iterative cooperation between AI and human economist that can do the most. And besides, if we automate the production of economic research, who is going to read all those papers, condense it into something humans can work with? The discussion, interpretation and  application will still involve humans.

That means we will need well-educated economists in the future, too. And it is a good time to remind ourselves how Keynes described the "master-economist": she must be mathematician, historian, statesman, philosopher, to a degree. She must understand symbols and speak in words. She must contemplate the particular in terms of the general, and touch abstract and concrete in the same flight of thought; ... be purposeful and disinterested in a simultaneous mood, as aloof and incorruptible as an artist, yet sometimes as near to earth as a politician.

It will be a while until AI can be all that.

If there is one reframing which could change the way we approach our economic malaise, it would be to replace the phrase 'the cost of living crisis' with something else: 'the cost of working crisis', perhaps, or, simpler still, 'the cost of trying crisis'.

Implicit in the phrase 'the cost of living' is the idea that the main task of government is to make sure that every-body can exist in a state of barely tolerable subsistence: a wonderful aspiration if you want to parade your moral credentials, but don't expect it to grow the economy.

Growth demands the very opposite of egalitarian subsistence: it emerges from discretionary risk, discretionary effort and discretionary spending.

✍️ Rory Sutherland

One of the greatest lessons Economics 



teaches as a social science is that human beings respond predictably to rewards, penalties, and constraints not to good intentions.

Think about what happens in real life:
 When price controls are forced on essential goods without addressing supply, scarcity and black markets appear overnight.
 When taxes or regulations are raised sharply without supporting local productivity, businesses quietly shift into the informal sector.

 When subsidies are poorly targeted, the people who need relief the least often capture the largest share.
Good economic thinking looks past what a policy promises on paper and asks one simple question: What behavior does this actually incentivize?
When you train yourself to analyze policies through incentives and unintended consequences, your essays, research papers, and policy arguments immediately carry weight.

content:
We trust GDP the way we trust a bathroom scale. It tells us something real, and we have quietly let it start answering questions it was never built for.

A scale will give you your weight with perfect honesty and say nothing about your health, your happiness, or whether you slept well last night. GDP does something similar. It totals up what changed hands for money, honestly and simply, and stays silent on everything else that mattered just as much, simply because it never had a price attached. That is not GDP lying to you, any more than the scale was lying when it said nothing about your sleep. It is just the limit of what you asked it to measure.

The habit worth questioning is not GDP itself, but how easily one honest number gets asked to answer a much bigger question, whether people's lives are actually getting better. Most of us have felt that gap at some point, between the figures and how economic life actually feels, even without having a name for it.

content:
Economics isn’t really about money.

It starts with something much simpler:

You can’t have everything.

We have unlimited wants, but the resources available to satisfy them are limited.

Money is limited.
⏰ Time is limited.
🧠 Attention is limited.
🌍 Natural resources are limited.

That mismatch is called Scarcity — and it’s where economics begins.

Because resources are scarce, we have to make choices. And whenever we choose one thing, we give up the opportunity to use those same resources somewhere else.

That’s why scarcity leads to trade-offs — whether you’re deciding how to spend an evening, how a business should use its budget, or how an economy should allocate its resources.

Money is only part of the story.

Scarcity is the condition. Choice is the consequence.

content:
Beyond the Scalar Standard

Can a single number really tell you what something is worth?

We treat money as if it were a universal yardstick of value. But here's a structural problem, not a practical one: no single number can capture multiple independent dimensions of value—physical, ecological, qualitative, social—without losing information. And this isn't a failure of clever aggregation methods. It's mathematically inevitable.

My new manuscript, Beyond the Scalar Standard, proves this along four independent mathematical routes. Whether prices are smooth, kinked, merely continuous, or come from a discrete catalogue—the information loss is structural. It also introduces a continuous, scaling-invariant "representation loss coefficient" to measure how blind a price system is to specific changes. No arbitrary thresholds. No arbitrary percentages.

The institutional implication is not to abolish money. Money remains essential for transactions. But we should separate:

· Payment (money as a medium of exchange),
· Measurement (objective, multidimensional profiles),
· Valuation (normative, explicit weighting).

This separation doesn't solve the problem—it makes it visible, measurable, and empirically testable. The manuscript is theoretical: it establishes a limit and proposes a diagnostic architecture. Empirical superiority of multidimensional systems remains an open research question.

If you work on monetary theory, ecological economics, value pluralism, or the limits of aggregation, I'd be glad to hear where you see the strongest connections—or the strongest objections.

content:
WHAT IS MACROECONOMICS?


Macroeconomics is the branch of economics that studies the behaviour and performance of an economy as a whole. Unlike microeconomics, which focuses on individual consumers, households, firms, and specific markets, macroeconomics examines aggregate economic variables and the overall functioning of an economy. It deals with major economic indicators such as Gross Domestic Product (GDP), national income, inflation, unemployment, interest rates, aggregate demand, and aggregate supply. Macroeconomics explains how these variables interact and influence economic growth, price stability, employment, and the general standard of living. For example, when an economy experiences a persistent increase in the general price level, macroeconomics analyses the causes of inflation and its effects on purchasing power, investment, savings, and economic welfare. Therefore, macroeconomics provides a comprehensive framework for understanding economic conditions and developments at the national and global levels.

The major areas of macroeconomic analysis include national income accounting, theory of employment, consumption and investment, money and banking, inflation and unemployment, business cycles, fiscal policy, monetary policy, and international economics. National income accounting measures the total economic output and income generated within an economy, particularly through indicators such as GDP and Gross National Income (GNI). The theory of employment examines the determinants of employment and unemployment, while consumption and investment analysis explains how households and businesses contribute to aggregate demand. Macroeconomics also studies the role of money, interest rates, banking institutions, and financial markets in influencing economic activity. Furthermore, fiscal policy examines how government taxation and public expenditure affect aggregate demand and economic performance, whereas monetary policy focuses on how central banks use interest rates and other monetary instruments to maintain price stability and influence economic activity. International macroeconomics additionally analyses exchange rates, balance of payments, international capital flows, and the relationship between domestic and global economic conditions.

In the contemporary world, macroeconomics plays a central role in economic planning, policymaking, financial stability, and sustainable development. Governments and central banks use macroeconomic theories and analytical tools to address challenges such as inflation, unemployment, recession, public debt, exchange rate instability, and slow economic growth. For example, during an economic recession, policymakers may increase public expenditure or reduce taxes to stimulate aggregate demand, while central banks may adjust interest rates to influence borrowing, investment, and consumption.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Economics explains why we need to rethink negotiation.

What does Nobel laureate Michael Woodford's research have to do with the billions of dollars companies negotiate every day?

Quite a lot, actually.

His work highlights something we have been arguing for years through NegoEconomics: economic outcomes are influenced by expectations, information, and the decisions people make.

Yet most companies still negotiate as if price is the most important variable.
Our negotiation research suggests that as much as 42% of potential economic value can be left on the table.

Not necessarily because negotiators are incompetent, but because they are focused on dividing value rather than discovering it.

We reward discounts. We celebrate concessions. We measure savings.

But how often do we measure the economic value we never discovered?
Woodford's Nobel Prize does not prove NegoEconomics. But his research offers an important intellectual connection to why traditional negotiation thinking may be economically inadequate.

I explore that connection in my new article.

Perhaps the biggest problem isn't that we negotiate bad deals. It's that we have become very good at negotiating deals without knowing how much better they could have been.

content:
Prices don't rise by accident . Two forces set them , and inflation starts when one of them breaks . 📊
Supply and demand set the price of almost everything :
▪️ Demand up, supply down → prices rise
▪️ Supply up, demand down → prices fall
Inflation appears when this balance breaks , usually in one of two ways :
1️⃣ Supply side : broken supply chains or higher production costs mean fewer goods for the same demand .
2️⃣ Money side : when the money supply grows faster than output, more money chases the same goods and the currency's purchasing power erodes .
Different causes , same result : your money buys less .
For investors and businesses , the first step is diagnosing which force is driving
 prices , because the response differs . Supply-side inflation calls for diversifying suppliers and reviewing contracts. Monetary inflation calls for protecting the real value of assets .

💬 How are current inflation waves affecting your financial plans or business operations?

[INFLATION]

This is the persistent increase in the price level of goods and services in the economy for a certain period of time.

NB:Price is a variable factor, which means it changes as output changes 

*Types of in INFLATION *

#Hyper-inflation 
This is the extreme form of inflation in which the general price level rises at a very fast rate.Eg the indecent in Germany between 1919 and 1923

#Suppressed inflation 
This is inflation whose rate of price increase and effect are controlled by the use of devices like price control and rationing
NB: This inflation is caused by excess demand over supply 

#Creeping inflation 
This is inflation, which moves very slow, but there are continuous increases in general price level

The above types of inflation are caused by price level

The following types of inflation are caused by Cause.

#Demand-pull inflation 
This is a situation in which aggregate demand persistently exceeds aggregate supply so that prices are being pulled upwards.
^Demand >Supply =Prices increase upward 
NB: This inflation occurs when there is full employment of resources.

#Cost-Push inflation 
This refers to a situation in which the cost of production is persistently rising so that prices are being pushed upwards 
^Cost of production >output=Price increase

#Cause of Demand-Pull inflation 
*increase in government expenditure 
Borrowing≠taxation =supply purchasing power that will lead to increased demand over supply 

*Increase supply of balance of payment 
Export earnings >Imports expenditure =excess income leading to increase demand over supply 

*Increase supply of money
increase in supply of money because of an increase in commercial banks' ability to create credit not marched by a corresponding increase in the rate of saving 

*Increase autonomous investment 
*etc

#Causes of cost-Push inflation 
*Higher wage claim
when trade unions plead for increased wage rate, employers may accept it, which will lead to an increased cost of production.

Inflation is one of the most important macroeconomic issues affecting individuals, businesses, and the overall economy.
It refers to a sustained increase in the general price level of goods and services over time.
There are two major types of inflation:
1.Demand-Pull Inflation: Occurs when aggregate demand exceeds the economy's productive capacity.
2.Cost-Push Inflation: Occurs when production costs increase, causing businesses to raise prices.
Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money, meaning consumers can buy fewer goods and services with the same amount of money.
Understanding inflation is essential for analyzing economic stability.

content:
I am very pleased to be able to share with you the Sustainable Economies Research Group's latest journal paper. 'On How Price Shocks Moderate Pro‐Environmental Social Norms for Sustainable Consumption'.  Please see the paper here: https://lnkd.in/e2W2f43D 

The work is highly important, as recent energy price shocks, related to the start of Russia's war against Ukraine in 2022, led to inflation levels not seen in several decades. Consumers had to pay much more for energy but also for essential goods, such as food and water. The unanticipated nature of this shift in price incentives has resulted in consumers not only to change their short-term consumption patterns but also their pro-environmental behaviours and social norms more generally. In light of current energy supply chain disruptions due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, energy price shocks have materialised once again.  From these shocks, there is already emerging evidence that households are motivated to implement pro-environmental behaviours, speeding up the transition to electrified mobility. If a currently elevated interest in electric vehicles (Jolly 2026) translates into a more permanent norm shift, the importance of prices in the context of social norms and pro-environmental behaviour cannot be overstated; this phenomenon requires timely in depth and robust study and this is what this paper provides.

The relationship between prices and pro-environmental social norms has not previously been studied.  This is a very new area of research.  We find that price changes result in a rational economic response, but also a social norms effect that has not been properly recognised, or acknowledged previously in the mainstream economics.  

As a result of the in depth empirical investigation we observe evidence of a strong  relationship. Building on this we develop and put forward a new theory: "price norm theory" that opens up an entirely new area of exploration in relation to social norms (and pro-environmental social norms) research.

The Economy is the Engine: A Calculus of Motion ⚙️📈

If we view human inquiry through the lens of calculus, how do we view the global economy?
In my latest conceptual framework, “The Economy is the Engine: A Calculus of Motion,” I map the principles of Economics to the mathematics of change:
🔹 Capital = Fuel [f(x)]: The latent potential energy. Whether financial, intellectual, or human, it remains inert without action.
🔹 Investment = The Spark [dy/dx]: Differentiation. It is the calculated decision made at a specific point in time to ignite growth and take calculated risks.
🔹 Economy = The Engine [∫]: Integration. The synthesis of all investment decisions over time—the accumulated kinetic energy that drives production, wealth, and societal progress.
🔹 Equilibrium = Engine Efficiency [C]: The Criterion of Sufficiency. Every engine has a "Redline." This is the point of maximum efficiency where risk and return (ROI) are perfectly balanced, preventing the engine from overheating (inflation) or stalling (recession).
The economy does not stop at integration; it is an infinite generative loop. To understand the engine, we must master the calculus of motion.

content:
The economist Anwar Shaikh died in October at the age of 80.

Anwar taught at the New School for Social Research from 1972 and chaired its economics department. His work challenged the core assumption of mainstream economics: that markets tend toward balance, and that crises are outside shocks. He showed instead that profit drives investment, that competition is a struggle in which firms cut costs at workers' expense, and that recurring crises come from inside capitalism itself. His book Capitalism: Competition, Conflict, Crises (Oxford, 2016) brought three decades of that work together, grounded in empirical evidence.

For those of us working toward an economy organized around people instead of profit, his work is foundational. FREE's founding president, Clara Mattei, was one of his students and colleagues. Her tribute in Jacobin describes what he gave us: an emancipatory economics.

Society, Freedom and the Purpose of the Economy: Are We Serving Humanity or Wealth?
What is the purpose of an economic system if it cannot adequately serve the people whose lives depend on it?
I recently finished reading Bernie Sanders' It's OK to Be Angry About Capitalism, and it got me thinking about some fundamental questions.

Why do we continue to witness extreme inequality in a world that generates so much wealth?
Why can businesses sometimes become more profitable by exploiting the very problems they claim to solve?
Why do workers often struggle to earn a decent living while companies continue to pursue ever-higher profits?
What role do corporate influence and political lobbying play in shaping economic policy?
And why should wealth give a handful of individuals disproportionate influence over political decisions that affect millions?

My concern is not with entrepreneurship, innovation or people becoming wealthy. It is with an economic arrangement in which the pursuit of profit can take precedence over human dignity, fair wages, social responsibility and the common good.
I also explore the relationship between corporate power, global resource exploitation, economic dependency, philanthropy and the responsibility of governments to provide meaningful welfare policies.

Drawing on the ideas of Martin Luther King Jr., Franklin D. Roosevelt and Gandhi, alongside contemporary research, I examine whether our economic systems are truly delivering the freedom and prosperity they promise.

I do not claim to have the perfect economic model. But I believe we should be willing to question the systems we have inherited and ask whether they are truly serving humanity.
An economy should be judged not merely by how much wealth it creates, but by how well it enables humanity to live, prosper and flourish.

I would welcome thoughtful perspectives, including those that challenge my arguments.

content:
THE ECONOMICS OF DEMOCRACY 

02 — What Does It Really Cost to Be Poor?

Imagine earning just enough to survive, but never quite enough to get ahead.

You go to the market with a carefully prepared budget. You know buying in bulk would be cheaper, but you cannot afford the upfront cost. So you buy in smaller quantities, paying more for what someone with greater purchasing power gets at a discount.

An unexpected expense comes along. Your savings are barely enough to absorb it. Another month begins, and the cycle continues.

This is one of the cruel ironies of poverty: it often costs more to have less.

Poverty is not merely the absence of money; it is also the absence of choices. It limits access to affordable credit, reliable transportation, quality healthcare and even the economies of scale that make everyday living cheaper.

Economists describe some of these constraints through the poverty trap and liquidity constraints. But behind these terms are people whose incomes are consumed by the very necessities they need to survive.

This is why the work of institutions such as the Centre for the Study of the Economies of Africa (CSEA), Nigerian Economic Summit Group (NESG) and the Nigerian Institute of Social and Economic Research matters. Understanding poverty requires more than measuring income; it requires examining the economic structures that perpetuate it.

We often ask why people struggle to save, invest or build wealth. Perhaps we should first ask how much of their income is left after the cost of being alive.

How can people build a better future when so much of their present is spent simply trying to survive?

Because the fight against poverty must be about more than helping people earn more. It must also be about creating an economy where having less does not mean paying more for almost everything.

— The Everyday Economist | Ene Favour Otinya

ECONOMIC ORTHODOXY OR COMMON SENSE?
We seem to have turned economics into a religion, with the Bank of England’s policymakers as its high priests. They interpret the numbers, pronounce their economic prophecies and prescribe the same ritual: raise interest rates and make everyone pay.

But here’s the problem.

When inflation is driven by external energy costs and supply-side pressures, how does making borrowing more expensive produce cheaper energy, increase productivity or bring down the cost of imports?

It doesn’t.

What it does do is squeeze household spending, increase business costs, discourage investment and put already struggling businesses and livelihoods under even greater pressure.
Interest rates have a place in tackling inflation driven by excessive demand. But applying the same medicine to every inflationary illness risks making the patient weaker rather than curing the disease.
We need less economic dogma and more economic common sense.
The real economy – businesses, jobs, investment and the people who sustain it – should not be sacrificed on the altar of economic orthodoxy.
Perhaps it’s time common sense had a seat at the table.

That challenges both respect for precedent and the German understanding of legal scholarship as a Wertungswissenschaft—an evaluative discipline.

Posner’s appeal, for me, is that he forces lawyers to explain why an inefficient rule deserves to survive. The challenge for us as economists is to recognise when there is a good answer.

Is Money Losing Its Real Value? Why Your Money Buys Less Than Before
Have you ever wondered why the same amount of money buys fewer goods and services today than it did a few years ago?
You may earn more, save more and even receive salary increases. Yet, your purchasing power may continue to decline.
This raises an important question: Are we actually becoming wealthier, or are we simply holding larger amounts of money with less real value?
One of the biggest challenges facing modern economies is the erosion of purchasing power.
Several factors contribute to this phenomenon:
🔹 Inflation: Rising prices reduce the amount of goods and services that money can purchase.
🔹 Monetary Policy: Interest rates and money supply decisions influence inflation, borrowing costs and the value of savings.
🔹 Government Debt: High levels of public debt can create long-term economic and monetary challenges.
🔹 Currency Depreciation: Weakening currencies make imported goods more expensive and can accelerate domestic inflation.
🔹 Income Inequality: People with limited savings and fixed incomes are often more vulnerable to rising living costs.
🔹 Savings Challenges: When returns on savings remain below inflation, the real value of accumulated wealth declines.
But there is another important dimension.
Money is not simply a medium of exchange. It is also a store of value and a foundation of trust in the economic system.
When people lose confidence in the purchasing power of money, their financial behavior changes. They may increasingly seek alternative assets such as real estate, gold, equities or other investments.
However, none of these alternatives is free from risk.
The real challenge is not simply earning more money. It is preserving the purchasing power of what we earn and save.
In my view, financial stability should be evaluated not only through nominal income, GDP growth or reported returns, but also through people's actual purchasing power and quality of life.
A growing economy does not necessarily mean that its citizens are becoming wealthier.
Perhaps the most important economic question today is not how much money we have, but what that money can actually buy.
What do you think? Is preserving purchasing power becoming more important than increasing income?

5 Key principle of Marketing psychology 

1. Emotion Drives Decisions – Connect your product with customers' feelings and desires.
2. Trust Builds Loyalty – Customers buy from brands they believe in.
3. Social Proof Influences Choices – People feel more confident when others recommend or use a product.
4. Perceived Value Matters – Customers consider the value they receive, not just the price they pay.
5. Convenience Encourages Purchase – Make it easy for customers to find, buy, and receive your products.

Successful marketing is not about convincing everyone to buy. It is about understanding what matters to customers and creating the right value to influence their decisions.

People may forget your advertisement, but they remember how your brand makes them feel.

Imagine this.

A restaurant publishes videos every day.

One video gets thousands of views.

People visit the profile. Some become interested. A few send messages.
But the number of actual customers barely changes.

What went wrong?

The business assumed that more attention would automatically create more sales.
But attention and conversion are two different things.

Let's look at four possible problems:
1. Unclear positioning
People see the content but don't understand why they should choose this business.
2. Weak customer journey
Interested visitors don't know where to go, what to choose, or what to do next.
3. Unclear offer
The business communicates its products or services without explaining their value.
4. Poor follow-up
Potential customers make inquiries, but nobody handles those inquiries consistently.

Before investing more time and money into content, examine what happens after people discover your business.

Sometimes the biggest opportunity isn't getting 10,000 more views.
It's helping the people who already discovered you take the next step.

document.title: The best marketing doesn't just get attention.

content:
Marketing doesn’t start with an idea. It starts with a diagnosis.

When a city plans its next metro station, the signage and the launch campaign come last. The real work happens much earlier: how people actually move, where congestion builds, which neighbourhoods are being left behind, what would make the network genuinely useful.

Marketing deserves the same rigour.

Why do customers buy once and never come back? Why does a premium restaurant struggle to charge premium prices? Why do we send friends to our local car mechanic for years, but never recommend a big service chain?

None of these is a communication problem by default. They are problems of behaviour, value, experience and perception. Content cannot fix what the business hasn’t diagnosed. Each one begins with a person, not a platform, and each deserves a genuine answer before a single word is written.

And yet marketing has slowly been reduced to its most visible output. We confuse the craft of making things with the discipline of deciding what’s worth making. When the diagnosis is skipped, the brief becomes “we need more content”, and the answer is always more noise.

A clever campaign is a skill. Knowing which problem deserves solving is judgement, and judgement is where the real value sits.

Before any brief is written, a better question is worth asking: what do people currently believe, feel or do that this business needs to change? Everything that follows, the message, the medium and the measure, grows from that answer.

A beautifully built station in the wrong place is still the wrong station. In the same way, a well-crafted message aimed at the wrong problem is just an expensive way to be ignored.

A brand doesn’t become relevant by speaking more often. It becomes relevant by understanding what matters to people, sometimes before they can put it into words themselves.

Advertising earns attention.
Marketing earns the reason to give it.

It may be time to stop judging the intelligence of marketing by the volume of its output.

Click-through rates, engagement, sales and brand growth are common metrics used to evaluate digital marketing. But I think success of a marketing campaign should also be measured in terms of its effect on people and society, too.  Here is one huge problem in this industry; the responsibility brands have towards consumers. Businesses gather personal information, rely on influencers and make targeted ads to sway buying habits. These tactics work, but sometimes they are dishonest and target unsuspecting groups or deceive consumers.  Equality, Diversity and Inclusion (EDI) should be a priority as well. Marketing campaigns shape self and other perceptions. Brands should reflect a variety of backgrounds, abilities and communities, not stereotypes.  The same applies to Sustainability as well as Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR). The environmental responsibility of companies should not be just a marketing ploy. What they do, from packaging to supply chains, should back up their claims.  Professional responsibility for me as a business development / digital marketing professional is to place a premium on honesty, consumer trust and commercial outcomes.  In my opinion, marketing shouldn't only sell people on purchasing a product, it should provide them with good reasons to trust a brand.

Before I recommend another campaign, I want to understand the customer, look closely at the data available, find the gaps, and be clear about what needs to change.

Because marketing strategy without customer understanding quickly turns into another round of expensive guessing.

That’s why I’m increasingly drawn to connecting customer research, product positioning, marketing intelligence, and growth strategy. Not as separate activities, but as one system that helps businesses make better decisions.

The goal isn’t to do more marketing. It’s to understand what will make the marketing work better.

One of the most important lessons I learned at NUMMI was the value of small teams where people could learn together.

Team members worked closely with their team leaders every day. They could discuss problems, ask questions, and even say, "I don't know what's causing this."

Leadership is often tested in the decisions nobody applauds.



It is easy to look decisive when the options are straightforward.

The real test comes when every available option has consequences.

When resources are limited.
When difficult conversations cannot be avoided.
When a popular decision is not necessarily the right business decision.
When the immediate pressure to deliver results conflicts with what the organisation needs in the long term.

These are the moments that reveal the quality of leadership.

At executive level, decision-making requires more than confidence. It requires sound judgement, an understanding of risk, the ability to consider different perspectives and the courage to take responsibility for outcomes.

Not every good decision will be popular.

Not every difficult decision will produce immediate results.

But leadership must always be guided by what serves the organization's long-term interests.

The quality of leadership is not measured only by the decisions people see, but also by the judgement behind them.

A POSITION OF LEADERSHIP IS NOT A LICENCE TO BE TOXIC.

Never become so comfortable in a position of authority that you begin to make life difficult for others simply because you have the power to do so.

The private sector can sometimes feel like the barracks, where people come, serve, grow and eventually move on. Some resign, some retire, and others are laid off. The truth is that no position is permanent, and no title lasts forever.

You may have the authority today, but tomorrow, circumstances can change.

Lead with empathy. Treat people well. Leave a positive legacy wherever you serve.

Because at the end of the day, the world is watching, and how you treat people matters.

• Effective leaders put the needs of others first.
• Humility means being willing to accept constructive feedback.
• Lasting influence comes from serving others and helping them succeed.

𝗦𝗵𝗲 𝗶𝗻𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗮 ₹𝟳,𝟮𝟬𝟬 𝗰𝗿𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗰𝗿𝗶𝘀𝗶𝘀. 𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝘀𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗱𝗻'𝘁 𝗶𝗻𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗱𝘀𝗲𝘁 𝗼𝗳 𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘂𝗽. 👇

 In 2019, Café Coffee Day founder V.G. Siddhartha passed away.

Behind him was a business facing a massive debt crisis of approximately ₹7,200 crore.

For most people, this would have been the end of the story.

But for Malavika Hegde, it became the beginning of a different fight.

She stepped forward when the business was at one of its most difficult moments.

No shortcuts. No overnight success. Just difficult decisions, patience and relentless determination.

And slowly, things started changing.

The company's debt reportedly came down from ₹7,200 crore in March 2019 to ₹3,100 crore by March 2020, and further to ₹1,731 crore by March 2021.

That's not just a financial turnaround.

That's an extraordinary example of resilience.

Here are 5 business lessons from her journey:

1. 𝐋𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐩 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐝𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚 𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐬. Anyone can lead when things are going well. Real leadership shows up when everything is falling apart.

2. 𝐍𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐟𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐚 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐭 𝐩𝐡𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐚 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐫𝐞.One bad chapter doesn't have to define the entire story.

3. 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐲 𝐛𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐬 𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐜. Big turnarounds are built through hundreds of difficult decisions.

4. 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐩𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞. Sometimes you have to step forward even when the situation feels bigger than you.

5. 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐛𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐚𝐝𝐯𝐚𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐠𝐞. The ability to keep moving when things get difficult can change the future of an entire organization

The biggest lesson?

𝐒𝐮𝐜𝐜𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐢𝐬𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐥𝐰𝐚𝐲𝐬 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐳𝐞𝐫𝐨. 𝐒𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐦𝐞𝐬, 𝐢𝐭'𝐬 𝐚𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐬𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐞𝐥𝐬𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐤𝐬 𝐢𝐬 𝐥𝐨𝐬𝐭.

Malavika Hegde's journey reminds us that leadership isn't about having all the answers.

It's about refusing to give up when the answers aren't clear.

What do you think matters more in business: intelligence, experience, or resilience?

I'd love to hear your thoughts. 👇

"It's not the product. It's not the service that you compete with. It's the organization in itself that will be the competitive advantage now."

Kjell A Nordström's words at Nordic Business Forum 2026 set the tone for one of the key questions leaders face right now: how should we build our organizations for what comes next?

We went through the talks and collected 10 practical lessons. Here are a few to get you started:

→ Reward experiments, not just successes. Steven Bartlett incentivizes the number of experiments, whether they succeed or fail, and moves fast on decisions that can be reversed.

→ Build a V2 of your company. Shawn Kanungo challenged leaders to stop adding AI on top of the old organization and imagine rebuilding it from a clean sheet.

→ Pair high challenge with high support. Angela Duckworth pointed out that individuals choose the culture they join, but leaders choose the culture they grow.

The full blog covers all 10 lessons, from heterarchies to tech audits, and each one comes with concrete next steps you can take with your team.

Many of my greatest lessons have come from watching my Dad in business.

This week, I spoke at the LBS Leadership Forum in Phoenix about what it means to be a player/coach, drawing on a lesson I learned from watching my Dad.

Imagine two HVAC business owners.

The first runs his business from a spreadsheet. He’s never been on a roof or worked on a unit. His bids are guesses. His guys realize nobody is checking their work, so standards slide. Leadership is weak, direction is unclear, and accountability is nonexistent.

The second is a master of his craft. A black belt in problem-solving. He stays on the cutting edge because he’s still doing the work. He walks into a room and knows what’s wrong almost immediately.

He has vision, works shoulder to shoulder with his team, and earns their respect because they know he’s one of them. He sets the standard for continuous improvement. Learning never ends.

Same industry. Same trucks. Totally different business.

My Dad is the second guy, and I’m blessed to have grown up watching him lead that way. It’s shaped how I approach mastering my own craft.

The standard of any organization starts with its leadership. How hard you work, how much you learn, and how much you care about being the best at what you do. Your people see all of it.

That’s what being a player/coach means to me.

content:
Yesterday, I imagined something.

What if someone invited me to give a 15-minute talk on personal branding?

What would I actually say?

After building my own brand and helping clients build theirs, I'd talk about these 6 things:

𝟭. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱?

A personal brand is the way you present yourself to the world. It reflects who you are, what you do, what you believe in, and what makes you different from others.

It's how people recognise you, understand your expertise, and form an opinion about you through your work, actions, and communication.

Simply put, it's the identity and reputation you build around your name.

𝟮. 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝘄𝗮𝗻𝘁 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲 𝗸𝗻𝗼𝘄𝗻 𝗳𝗼𝗿?

Before building your personal brand, you need to know what you want people to associate your name with.

Are you a designer, a strategist, a coach, or a founder? What expertise do you want people to recognise you for?

Give people a clear idea of what you do.

𝟯. 𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗮 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗿𝗲𝗳𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘀 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱.

Once you know what you want to be known for, make sure your LinkedIn profile communicates it.

When someone visits your profile, they should quickly understand who you are, what you do, who you help, and what makes your work valuable.

Your headline, banner, About section, and experience should all tell the same story.

content:
A strong personal brand on LinkedIn does not begin with a large follower count.
It begins with clarity, credibility, and consistency.

Many professionals wait until they have enough experience, achievements, or recognition before they start sharing their thoughts online.

But building a professional identity is a process. You develop it by showing up, sharing what you know, and contributing to conversations in your industry.

If you are starting with zero followers, here are five principles to help you build your personal brand:
1. Define your focus
- Identify your target audience.
- State the problem you help solve.
- Choose one area of expertise.
A clear focus makes your professional identity easier to understand and remember.

2. Present a credible profile
Your profile is often the first thing people see before exploring your content.
- Use a professional, approachable photograph.
- Write a headline that communicates your value.
- Create a concise summary of your professional journey.
Your headline is your first impression. Make it count.

3. Establish content pillars
Give your content a clear structure through three recurring themes:
- What you are learning.
- Lessons from your experiences.
- Your considered opinions.
This gives your audience a reason to return to your profile.

4. Contribute before you publish
Visibility also comes from participating in conversations.
- Comment on five relevant posts every day.
- Share insights instead of generic praise.
- Build meaningful relationships through your comments.
Be useful in the conversations happening within your industry.

5. Document your journey
You do not need to be an industry authority to share valuable insights.
- Publish three times every week.
- Share both results and lessons.
- Review which posts generate meaningful responses.
Consistency builds trust faster than perfection.

The Tension Between Results and Relationships

Are you naturally more focused on getting results or building relationships? Most leaders have a bias towards one or the other. The challenge is learning to balance both.

In this episode of World's Greatest Business Thinkers, Mark Miller, founder of Lead Every Day and a Wall Street Journal bestselling author on leadership, shares an interesting observation from more than 20 years of teaching leadership around the world.

Mark estimates that around 95% of leaders have a natural preference for either results or relationships. Neither orientation is wrong, but leaning too heavily towards one can create tension and undermine leadership effectiveness.

The best leaders understand that achieving results and building strong relationships aren't competing priorities. They need both. The challenge is recognising your natural bias and deliberately developing the side that doesn't come as easily.

The biggest lesson: Great leadership isn't about choosing between results and relationships. It's about learning to balance both, even when one comes more naturally than the other.

content:
What I've learned after gaining 2.5 MILLION impressions on LinkedIn in the space of 10 months. 

Just have fun.
No seriously, that's it.. 

I think we've made personal branding SO unnecessarily complicated.

You need 5 content pillars, a strict posting schedule, a perfectly defined niche, you have to engage for 30 minutes before posting, like your own post and ask three questions in the comments.

WHO IS MAKING THESE RULES???

In the last 10 months, I've gained over 2.5 million impressions on LinkedIn.

And do you know what I've been doing?

Posting memes.
Leaving unhinged comments on people's posts.
Sharing random quotes that pop into my head.
Celebrating follower milestones with pictures of absolutely INSANE amounts of food.
And posting whatever I feel like talking about that day.

I don't force myself to post when I have nothing to say.

I don't panic if I miss a day. 

Because somewhere along the way, I think we forgot that personal branding is supposed to be PERSONAL.

Of course, having a strategy can work.

But so can showing up as yourself, sharing things you genuinely enjoy and actually having a bit of fun with it.

Not every post needs to educate, inspire or position you as a thought leader.

Sometimes people just want to laugh.

Sometimes they want to relate.

2.5 million impressions later, I'm still convinced of one thing.

Fun IS a marketing strategy.

And it's probably my favourite one.

content:
Something I've noticed about some brands on LinkedIn.....


People can see what you post, know what you sell and still have no idea why they should choose you.

Truth is, that's a branding problem.
And here are four things I often notice:


• You talk about your services but don't explain what makes your approach different.

• You share industry tips but don't connect them to the problems your customers actually pay you to solve.

• Your LinkedIn profile says one thing, but your content tells a completely different story.

• Your messaging keeps changing, so people struggle to associate your brand with one specific solution.


Now, if a founder came to me with these challenges, here's where I'd start:


• First, I'd understand what their profile, messaging and content currently communicate.

• Second, I'd identify what's missing, unclear or inconsistent in their content. 

• Third, I'd establish their value, audience and what differentiates them from other brands. 

• And lastly, I'd study what's working, then strengthen their brand through strategic content and storytelling.


Because posting more isn't always the answer.

Sometimes, your brand doesn't need more content. 
What it needs is a clearer message.

Let me hear from you.

Business coaches, your LinkedIn comments are part of your personal brand.

And most people are wasting that opportunity.

If your comments are only:

Great post!

Absolutely agree.

So true 👏

…you’re getting visibility without showing your expertise.

Instead, use your comments to make people curious about how you think.

Try this 3-part comment formula:

1. Add a perspective
Don’t repeat the post. Share what you see differently.

2. Give a quick example
Bring the idea into a real situation you’ve experienced.

3. Leave a thought worth remembering
End with a short insight that makes someone stop scrolling.

For example:

Instead of:

Great point about leadership.

Try:

Leadership becomes difficult when you’re trying to be liked by everyone on your team. I’ve found that clear expectations often create more trust than trying to avoid uncomfortable conversations.

Now your comment does more than support someone else’s post.

It shows people how you think.

And that’s what personal branding is supposed to do.

If you're a business coach trying to build authority on LinkedIn, start treating your comments as part of your content strategy not an afterthought.

content:
Building your personal brand on top of your 9-5 job  🤔 

As I’ve become more intentional about sharing my ideas, experiences and what I’m learning on LinkedIn, I’ve sometimes wondered how it looks from my employer’s perspective.

Will they think I’m looking for another job? Building something on the side? More interested in my own brand than my company’s?

Yet we know the benefits of building a professional reputation.

In my case, it has helped people understand what I am good at. Through sharing, it has helped me build credibility, and gain new opportunities and and experiences beyond my current job title, for instance facilitating AI Career Workshops.

And a good personal brand can benefit your employer too. When employees share useful perspectives and demonstrate expertise, that can reflect positively on the organisations they work for.

During a recent career coaching conversation where I shared these thoughts and doubts, I came to the realization that I just needed to talk to my manager about it, rather than worrying about what my employer might think.

I did that and was glad it went well. As long as the boundaries around confidentiality, conflicts of interest and representing your employer well, are not crossed, there are no issues with building your profile.

And I hope that all other employers understand that: One can be committed to their employer and still invest in a professional reputation that belongs to them.

Thus if concern about your employer’s reaction is holding you back from sharing your expertise, perhaps the first step is an open conversation.

Happy personal brand building!

You didn’t spend 15 years building a company just to become a full time LinkedIn creator.

But somehow, that’s what a lot of personal branding advice expects from CEOs.

Post every morning.

Comment on 50 posts.

Share your breakfast.

Tell everyone what you learned at the gym.

Record videos every day.

And apparently, if you don’t do all of that, you’re missing out on business.

I disagree.

Imagine you’re running a company doing $20 million in annual revenue.

You have employees.

Customers.

Budgets.

Important decisions.

And a business that needs your attention.

You don’t need another job creating content for strangers.

You need the right people to understand why your company is worth doing business with.

Those are very different objectives.

A founder’s LinkedIn presence should help answer questions a serious buyer is already asking.

Does this person understand my industry?

Do they have a credible point of view?

What has their company actually achieved?

Would I trust them with an important business problem?

And how do I start a conversation?

You don’t need to share every detail of your life to answer those questions.

You need a clear position.

Relevant expertise.

Credible proof.

And a way to reach the people who can buy.

That’s the kind of personal branding I believe in.

At Brandastics, we help founders develop that presence and connect it with targeted outreach and business development.

The goal isn’t to turn a CEO into a content creator.

It’s to make their expertise work for the business, even when they’re busy running it.

Because the best personal brand shouldn’t demand more of the founder’s time than the opportunities it creates are worth.

❯ Trust can come from outlier technical talent, from years spent serving the segment, or from a founder who gets industry leaders to back them early.
 
❯ Sumary showed those signals when we backed them at pre-seed. Through cold outreach, they had already put CEOs of the bookkeeping firms they wanted as customers on their advisory board.
 
❯ Winners don’t lead with a perfect ROI case or the biggest product. They make it easy for customers to say yes, starting with the contract and the first use case.
 
❯ That first use case should be exciting enough to want and narrow enough that nobody’s whole AI bet rests on it.

content:
She left her high-paying job at PayPal in the US to build a fintech company in India.

Meet Upasana Taku, co-founder of Mobikwik and India's first female fintech leader.

In 2008, she had a stable corporate career that lakhs of people dream of, but she wanted to contribute to India's growing startup ecosystem.

When she returned to India, she worked with a rural microfinance NGO in Bihar and Uttar Pradesh.

This helped her understand local communities and the challenges people faced.
She also noticed a gap in digital payments.

At the time, people often visited nearby shops to recharge their mobile phones. Using a digital wallet for everyday payments was still relatively new.

Upasana saw an opportunity to simplify these transactions. Together with Bipin Preet Singh, they co-founded MobiKwik in 2009.

What started as a mobile recharge platform gradually expanded into digital wallets, bill payments, consumer credit and other financial services.

In 2021, MobiKwik became a unicorn. In December 2024, it went public.

Today, the company serves over 193 million registered users and more than 5 million merchants.

The lesson from Upasana's journey?

She didn't start by following a trend. She started with a problem people faced every day.

Sometimes, the strongest business ideas come from understanding a problem others have learned to live with.

content:
I recently interviewed a founder who completely challenged the way I think about starting a business.

Liam Whittaker entered the fine jewellery industry with absolutely no experience in jewellery.

Before he'd even launched his website, he'd generated nearly $500,000 in sales!

What fascinated me wasn't just the number, it was his approach;

Most people think starting a business means building a brand, launching a website, perfecting your product and THEN finding customers. But Liam did almost the exact opposite.

He found customers first, listened to what they wanted, tested the market and then he built the business around what he'd learnt.

It challenged something we often take for granted in entrepreneurship: that you need to have everything in place before you're ready to launch.

Sometimes your customers can teach you more about building a successful business than months of planning ever will.

I loved this conversation with Liam the founder of HEIREST on the Make It Happen Podcast.

I'd love to know: would you launch a business before you had a website?

content:
Getting into a Founder's Office role at a startup is very easy. Follow my step-by-step path that got me here: 

> After school, randomly switch majors from science to finance for college
> At 17, do your first (unpaid) internship at a Non-profit 
> At 18, do a market research intern and find out what consulting is
> At 18 again, work with a CXO of a F500 company and write a scientific paper
> Then move cities to work at a fintech, cold call founders every day, and discover your love for startups
> At 19, skip college placements or any rational safe option and convince an early-stage startup to let you lead their growth initiatives

And there you go, you can be in a founder's office role too!

Point being, careers are anything but linear. Instead of focusing on what domain, company, or geography, you should try to define what you do and don't want to work on as early as you can. The only way to do that is to do more new things. 

I still think a lot about 'where I see myself in 5 years', but the only way I will know that is if I do a lot in the present.

Ram was the founding member of Microsoft’s digital transformation group. He led finance transformation projects for Fortune 500 companies, including Walmart and Coca-Cola.

content:
That app isn’t a bank. So who actually holds your money?

Here’s what happens when you open a fintech account:

You sign up in the app.

1. The app sends your details to a BaaS platform through an API.
2. The platform passes them to a sponsor bank for the KYC check.
3. The sponsor bank, the licensed one, opens the account and issues the card.
4. Money moves in through the card network and payment rails, then back          through the bank and the platform to your balance.
5. Everyone’s records have to match, every day.
6. Deposit insurance covers a bank failure, not a fintech failure.

The app is the face. The sponsor bank is the license. The platform is the plumbing.

Did you know your fintech balance isn’t held by the app?

FINANCIAL DISCIPLINE IS A FORM OF SELF-RESPECT

Financial discipline doesn’t mean denying yourself everything you enjoy. It means making decisions today that protect the future you are trying to build.

Sometimes discipline looks like:
* Choosing not to buy something immediately.
* Saving before spending.
* Sticking to your budget.
* Avoiding unnecessary debt.
* Walking away from an investment you don’t understand.

Financial progress rarely comes from one big decision. It is often built by small, disciplined decisions repeated consistently.

Remember:
Your financial future is influenced by the habits you practise today.

To be or  not to be: yes, we can! But... INTEGRATING FINANCIAL INNOVATION WITH SHARED PROSPERITY

By Moisès Roberto Escobar
https://lnkd.in/ed6N_2VZ
Colproce El Salvador 
Fundación para el Desarrollo de Centroamérica - FUDECEN 

The greatest opportunity of tokenization is not replacing traditional finance, but intelligently integrating its institutional strengths with blockchain, programmable assets, interoperable infrastructure and responsible digital innovation.

A comprehensive approach must align technology, financial institutions, government regulation, legal certainty, cybersecurity, transparency and human development.

The Bank for International Settlements (2025) highlights the potential of unified financial infrastructure to improve payments and securities markets. However, the OECD (2025) acknowledges that tokenization adoption remains limited, while the Financial Stability Board (2024) warns of emerging liquidity, operational and interconnectedness risks.

The strategic opportunity is to build an ecosystem that:

- Expands responsible access to productive capital, particularly for SMEs.
- Reduces intermediation costs and improves market efficiency.
- Strengthens competition, transparency and institutional accountability.
- Protects investors, consumers and financial stability.
- Distributes the benefits of innovation more equitably.

My reflection: Financial transformation should not be measured by how much technology we adopt, but by how effectively we combine it with sound institutions to improve productivity, opportunity, resilience and quality of life.

Innovation creates potential. Integration, governance and shared value turn that potential into sustainable development.

Technology must serve the economy, and the economy must serve society.

🌍 THE WORLD ON PAUSE: Is the Global Economy Becoming Too Dependent on Technology?
What happens when the digital systems we rely on suddenly stop working?
In just a few days, we witnessed:
🔹 Major disruptions to Microsoft services
🔹 Thousands of cancelled flights across the United States
🔹 Technical failures affecting banking transactions
🔹 Further operational disruption at United Airlines
These were separate incidents, with no verified evidence of a coordinated cause.
But together, they raise a much bigger question:
Have we built a global economy that is more connected and efficient — but also more vulnerable?
Today, banking, aviation, financial markets, businesses and governments depend on increasingly interconnected digital infrastructure.
At the same time, artificial intelligence, digital currencies and the concentration of technology providers are reshaping how our economies operate.
And this raises important questions about financial stability, cybersecurity, economic resilience and public trust.
💡 A financial crisis doesn't necessarily have to begin with a banking collapse or a stock market crash. Could the next major disruption begin with the technology that supports them?
In my latest article, I explore how these events connect to wider economic risks — from inflation and financial markets to digital currencies and the ongoing debate surrounding The Great Reset.
The aim is not to promote speculation but to distinguish verified facts from assumptions and understand the real risks facing an increasingly digital world.
Because in today's global economy, resilience may be just as important as growth.

Income matters. But it does not tell the whole story of people’s material living conditions.

Carla Oliveira Henriques, Oscar David Marcenaro-Gutierrez, Luis Alejandro Lopez-Agudo and Sara Sousa develop a multidimensional composite index combining income, poverty, material deprivation, inequality and housing conditions across European countries and over time.

Using window data envelopment analysis, the authors find persistent gender differences. Men consistently achieve higher levels of material living conditions, while women would require greater improvements in income and reductions in severe material deprivation to reach comparable levels.

The findings offer an important reminder: progress in one dimension can coexist with disadvantages in others. Understanding living conditions therefore requires going beyond income alone.

content:
What Is Money, Really?

Money is often described as a measure of value, a medium of exchange, a unit of account, and a store of value. While the wording has evolved over centuries, the core idea has remained remarkably consistent: money is a social invention that allows complex economies to function efficiently.

As a medium of exchange, money eliminates the inefficiencies of barter. Instead of finding someone who both has what you want and wants what you have, money serves as a universally accepted intermediary.

As a unit of account, money provides a common standard for pricing goods, services, assets, and labor. Whether buying a loaf of bread, a home, or a company, money gives us a shared language to compare value.

As a store of value, money allows purchasing power to be transferred through time. It enables people to save today and spend tomorrow. A currency that rapidly loses value through inflation fails this test and loses public confidence.

As a measure of value, money helps society quantify economic worth. While value itself is subjective, money provides a practical yardstick that allows markets to function.

Has this definition changed over the years? Not fundamentally. From gold and silver coins in ancient civilizations, to paper notes issued by governments, to today's digital bank deposits and electronic payments, the form of money has changed dramatically, but its essential functions have not.

What has changed is our understanding of money. Economists now view money less as a physical object and more as a system of trust. A dollar bill has little intrinsic value. Its worth comes from collective confidence that others will accept it in exchange for goods and services.

In the digital age, this evolution continues. Credit cards, mobile payments, cryptocurrencies, and central bank digital currencies challenge the traditional notion that money must be tangible. Increasingly, money is becoming information rather than an object.

Perhaps the most profound realization is that money is not wealth itself. Wealth consists of productive assets, skills, knowledge, businesses, technology, and natural resources. Money is simply the mechanism we use to measure, exchange, and store claims on that wealth. The distinction is subtle but important: societies become prosperous by creating wealth, not merely by creating more money.

Interest rates, inflation, currency movements, international trade and geopolitical developments are interconnected.

For business leaders, understanding these changes is no longer optional.
A change in currency value can influence import costs.

A change in interest rates can affect expansion decisions and capital investment.
Changes in international trade policies can reshape supply chains.

And economic uncertainty can influence customer spending and investor confidence.
This is why I believe business leaders should look beyond their company's internal performance.

They should continuously understand the external economic environment.

In my view, five questions deserve attention in every leadership discussion:

Are we prepared for changes in global demand?

How exposed is our business to currency fluctuations?

Are our investments aligned with long-term economic opportunities?

Can our operations remain resilient during uncertainty?

Are we identifying opportunities while others are focused only on risks?

Strong businesses don't control the economy. They build the ability to respond intelligently to it.

In today's interconnected world, economic awareness is an important part of business leadership.

The Illusion of Infinite Growth: Are We Innovating, or Just Optimizing?
Look at the headlines across continents today: cost-of-living protests in Europe, a mounting jobs crisis in India, and anti-tax uprisings in Kenya.

We are living through a synchronized global fracture. But this unrest isn't a temporary political failure—it is the mathematical conclusion of a broken financial system colliding with the illusion of modern innovation.

Here is the core trap: 
1️⃣ The Debt-Growth Treadmill: Almost all money is born as debt-with-interest. Because loans demand back more than was created, the macroeconomic system must expand infinitely just to pay off yesterday's interest. It's a treadmill that can never stop. 
2️⃣ The Innovation Trap (Optimization vs. Creation): To feed the debt treadmill, we chase tech breakthroughs like AI and automated farming. But these technologies don't create new human needs—they merely optimize existing ones. Because human biology caps our consumption (no one can eat twice as much food just because a machine harvests it faster), optimization eliminates labor without creating new economic space. 
3️⃣ The Tollbooth Economy: When physical utility saturates and true growth stalls, capital stops building the future and retreats into rent-extraction—buying up housing, infrastructure, and setting up subscriptions while using the "buy, borrow, die" loophole to avoid taxes.

You cannot endlessly tax "efficiency" to pay off exponential debt.

content:
Are we building an economy where people can live, or merely survive?
We have more technology, more innovation, more businesses and more wealth than ever before.

Yet millions of people are struggling to achieve something as basic as financial security.
People work for decades but struggle to afford homes.
Qualified professionals worry about losing their jobs.
Businesses celebrate record profits while employees worry about their next paycheck.
Automation is increasing productivity, but who actually benefits from that productivity?
The middle class is working harder to maintain its position, while wealth continues to concentrate in fewer hands.

Perhaps the problem isn't that the world isn't producing enough wealth. Perhaps it's how that wealth is distributed.
We need to rethink what economic progress actually means.
Is it simply higher GDP, bigger corporations and technological advancement?
Or should progress also mean:
Affordable housing and healthcare.
Financial security beyond employment.
Equal access to quality education.
Fair opportunities regardless of family wealth.
Technology that benefits society as a whole.

An economy should exist to serve people, not the other way around.
The real measure of progress should be how comfortably the majority of people can live, not just how wealthy the richest can become.

content:
Perhaps the greatest illusion of modern civilisation is that economic growth is a natural condition rather than a historical exception. For centuries, humanity lived within relatively stable material limits. The extraordinary expansion of the modern economy was made possible by an exceptional inheritance: abundant fossil energy, accessible resources and ecosystems capable of absorbing an extraordinary amount of extraction.
Nate Hagens asks: what happens when financial promises keep multiplying while the physical foundations required to honour them become increasingly constrained?
The danger is not simply resource scarcity. It is the collision of financial expectations, ecological limits, geopolitical fragmentation and political instability. Money can create claims on future prosperity, but it cannot manufacture the energy, materials or natural systems that make prosperity possible.
The real challenge, therefore, is not how to preserve growth at any cost, but how to preserve human flourishing when perpetual expansion is no longer a credible assumption. Civilisation must learn to distinguish progress from growth before reality makes that distinction for us.

content:
🌍 Indicators of Economic Development: Measuring a Nation's Progress

How do we determine whether a country is truly developing?

Economic development is not measured by GDP alone. It involves improvements in people's income, education, healthcare, living standards, and overall well-being.

Here are six important indicators of economic development:

1. GDP per Capita: Measures the average economic output per person and provides an indication of income levels.

2. Human Development Index (HDI): Measures development through three dimensions: health, education, and standard of living.

3. Poverty Rate: Shows the proportion of the population living below the poverty line.

4. Literacy Rate: Reflects educational progress and access to learning opportunities.

5. Life Expectancy: Indicates the overall health conditions and quality of healthcare.

6. Industrialization: Measures the growth and development of the industrial sector.

📊 Why Are These Indicators Important?

- Help governments develop effective economic policies.
- Allow comparisons between developed and developing countries.
- Identify economic and social challenges.
- Support inclusive and sustainable development.

My Key Takeaway:

A country's real progress is not simply about producing more wealth; it is about improving the quality of life of its people.

Economic development means creating opportunities, reducing poverty, and building a better future for everyone.

Doughnut Economics Explained

Developed by economist Kate Raworth, doughnut economics offers a simple picture of a sustainable economy. Key ideas from this short video:

1. Social foundation: no one should fall short on essentials such as food, health and education.
2. Ecological ceiling: economic activity must stay within the planet's boundaries.
3. The safe and just space between the two rings is where societies can thrive.
4. Cities like Amsterdam are already applying the model to real policy.

Growth alone is not the goal; balance between human needs and planetary limits is.

"I can't raise this for you."

I watched an advisor say this to a founder recently. The founder went quiet.

Two advisors offer to help you raise:
→ One says, "We'll get you funded."
→ The other says, "This isn't fundable yet."

Most founders pick the first. It's the answer they came for.

The first one sends your deck to every investor on the list. Most pass. And an investor who has passed rarely looks again soon.

The second one tells you what to fix before anyone sees it. It stings. It's also why your next attempt works.

Working in investment banking taught me one thing about advice: a "yes" costs nothing to say. A "no" can cost the person saying it the mandate.

That's exactly why it's worth listening to.

Founders: what's the hardest "no" you've heard that turned out to be right? 👇

content:
Can a Startup Raise More Money Than It Actually Needs?

Imagine your startup needs $2 million to reach its next growth milestone, but an investor offers you $5 million.

Should you take the larger amount?

At first glance, accepting the offer seems reasonable. Additional capital gives the company more flexibility to manage risks and pursue new opportunities.

But there is another side to consider.

When funding becomes available before a company has validated its business model, it may expand faster than it should.

It might enter new markets, hire larger teams, or significantly increase marketing spending before confirming that its existing product can generate sustainable revenue.

In that situation, funding does not only accelerate growth. It can also accelerate the consumption of resources.

That is why I believe the starting point for a funding decision should be the milestone the company needs to achieve, rather than the maximum amount it can raise.

Is the capital needed to test a product? Reach a specific number of customers? Or demonstrate the ability to generate recurring revenue?

Each stage comes with different capital requirements and risks.

Of course, raising more money can be justified, particularly when future funding opportunities are uncertain.

The question is not whether less funding is always better, but whether the amount raised is appropriate for the company's current stage and circumstances.
